Mamenchisaurus hatchlings emerging from the nest would have been extraordinarily vulnerable, beginning life at a wet weight at birth of approximately 10,000 grams [Wwb = approximately 10,000 grams]. This substantial neonatal mass, while large compared to most extant reptiles, represents a mere fraction of the prodigious size these sauropods would ultimately attain. Within the sauropodomorph lineage, an initial body size of this magnitude likely conferred a degree of protection against small predators from the moment of hatching. The transition from lecithotrophic dependence on the yolk to active foraging must have occurred rapidly, as the growing juvenile required immense amounts of plant material to fuel its accelerated growth phase. Field estimates for related macronarian sauropods suggest that neonatal mass in this range is consistent with a reproductive strategy involving relatively small clutch sizes but large individual eggs, a pattern that prioritizes offspring quality over quantity. The leathery-shelled eggs that contained these embryos would have required substantial investment from the gravid female, representing a significant allocation of resources directed toward offspring production. Such a high initial mass at birth (approximately 10,000 grams) [Wwb = approximately 10,000 grams] would have necessitated a long incubation period, during which the developing embryo was entirely dependent on the nutrients stored within the yolk-laden egg.

The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown Mamenchisaurus individual is estimated to have reached approximately 30,000,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 30,000,000 grams], placing it among the most massive terrestrial vertebrates ever to have existed. Reaching this truly gigantic asymptotic mass required a prolonged period of somatic growth, likely spanning several decades, during which the animal consumed vast quantities of ferns, cycads, and conifers. The energetic demands of sustaining this bodymass would have been immense, requiring a peak food intake rate that few contemporary ecosystems could support. Histological studies of limb bone cross-sections from related taxa suggest that growth was not constant but occurred in distinct annual cycles, with periods of rapid mass increase alternating with slower growth phases during resource-limited seasons.

It is likely that a female Mamenchisaurus would have been several decades old before she produced her first egg clutch, a reproductive schedule that demands exceptionally high adult survival rates to offset the delayed onset of breeding.

When a female Mamenchisaurus finally reached reproductive age, her annual reproductive output was necessarily constrained by her immense size and the long developmental period required for each offspring. A single annual nesting event each year was consistent with the pattern observed in large extant reptiles such as crocodilians and large tortoises, which also exhibit slow life histories. Each nesting season, the female would have excavated a substantial nest cavity, deposited the fertilised ova, and covered them with vegetation to provide incubation through the heat of microbial decomposition. Such a slow reproductive output would have required immense, stable habitats with abundant food resources to sustain viable populations over geological timescales.
